analogy.p: Scrooge is a driver heading down a road that ends in a lonely grave. Marley is the warning light on the dashboard. The three Spirits are like a sat-nav showing where he started (Past), where he is now and who is affected by his driving (Present), and exactly where the road leads if he carries on (Yet To Come). Because they are 'shadows of the things that May be', he can still turn the wheel. Stave 5 is him taking a new route and enjoying the journey. Where it breaks down: a sat-nav is neutral and just gives directions, but Scrooge's change is emotional and moral; he has to feel shame, grief and love. Also, changing route costs a driver nothing, but Scrooge must actively **make amends** for past harm ('back-payments'). Finally, a sat-nav helps only the driver, while Scrooge's new route changes other people's lives too, saving Tiny Tim.
analogy.t: The sat-nav that recalculates the route

bullets: The whole plot is a **redemption arc**: sin (Stave 1), confrontation with the past, present and future (Staves 2 to 4), repentance and reward (Stave 5).

The theme is **Christian** at its core: sin, **penitence** (being truly sorry), confession and a new life. Stave 5 is set on Christmas Day, the celebration of Christ's birth and of the Christian promise of salvation.
Dickens makes Scrooge **old** on purpose: the message is that redemption is open to **anyone, at any age**.
Redemption is not just a feeling. Scrooge must **make amends**: give to charity, raise Bob's salary, help Tiny Tim, rejoin his family.
Dickens's Preface hopes the 'Ghostly little book' will 'haunt their houses pleasantly': the readers are meant to be 'haunted' and transformed, just like Scrooge.
Link to other themes (context only): transformation is shown through the change from **greed to generosity**, **isolation to community**, and **cold to warmth**.

callouts.p: Being saved from sin, error or evil, usually by recognising wrongdoing, repenting and making amends.
A thorough or dramatic change in a character's nature, attitudes and behaviour.
Scrooge's personal transformation is a **microcosm** (small-scale model) of the social transformation Dickens wanted in Victorian England.

core.h: 1. What the theme means and why Dickens built the whole novella around it
core.p: **Redemption** means being saved from sin or from the consequences of past wrongs. **Transformation** means a complete change in character. In A Christmas Carol (1843) these two ideas are linked: Scrooge's inner **transformation** (cold to warm, selfish to generous) is the route to his **redemption** (he escapes Marley's fate and his own lonely, unmourned death). Dickens's bigger aim is to transform his **readers**. Scrooge stands for the wealthy, uncaring middle and upper classes of 1840s Britain, so if Scrooge can change, society can too.

bullets: 'a squeezing, wrenching, grasping, scraping, clutching, covetous old sinner!': a **list of present participles** (verbs ending -ing) suggests a man constantly grabbing money; the **asyndetic list** piles up his faults. The noun **'sinner'** introduces the religious frame: a sinner can be saved.

'Hard and sharp as flint, from which no steel had ever struck out generous fire': **simile**. Flint CAN spark fire when struck, so Dickens hints that warmth is hidden inside Scrooge and could be released. This **foreshadows** his transformation.

'secret, and self-contained, and solitary as an oyster': **polysyndeton** and **sibilance** stress isolation; an oyster is closed and hard but may contain a **pearl**, another hint of hidden goodness.
'The cold within him froze his old features': **pathetic fallacy turned inwards**; the coldness is moral, not physical.
'Bah! Humbug!': he rejects Christmas and therefore rejects the Christian values of generosity and goodwill.

'If they would rather die, they had better do it, and decrease the surplus population.': he echoes **Malthusian** ideas; these exact words are thrown back at him in Stave 3, which is a key structural device of his redemption.
'Are there no prisons?' ... 'And the Union workhouses?': **rhetorical questions** show his faith in the harsh **1834 Poor Law**.
He frightens away a boy singing a carol and grudges Bob a tiny fire and a day off.

callouts.p: Point out that even in Stave 1 Dickens plants **seeds of redemption** (flint can spark, oysters hold pearls). This shows the transformation is planned, not random.
Do not describe Scrooge as simply 'evil'. Dickens presents him as a **sinner** who has chosen a wrong path and can be saved. This is a crucial difference for this theme.

core.h: 2. The 'before': Scrooge in Stave 1 (why he needs redeeming)
core.p: Dickens makes Scrooge as unredeemable as possible at the start so that his change is more dramatic and his message more powerful: if even this man can change, anyone can. Scrooge is defined by **greed, coldness, isolation and contempt for the poor**.

bullets: 'I wear the chain I forged in life... I made it link by link, and yard by yard; I girded it on of my own free will': the chain is a **symbol** of sin, made of 'cash-boxes, keys, padlocks, ledgers'. The verb **'forged'** and the phrase **'of my own free will'** stress **personal responsibility**: we build our own punishment, so we can also choose to change.

'Mankind was my business. The common welfare was my business; charity, mercy, forbearance, and benevolence, were all my business.': Marley redefines 'business'. True business is **caring for others**, which is Dickens's central moral.
'no space of regret can make amends for one life's opportunity misused!': redemption must happen **in life**; after death it is too late.
'You have yet a chance and hope of escaping my fate.': Marley offers **hope**, so the redemption plot begins.
The phantoms outside the window are wailing because they 'sought to interfere, for good, in human matters, and had lost the power for ever': again, it will be too late after death.
Scrooge's first reaction is denial ('Humbug!', 'an undigested bit of beef'), showing that transformation will be a **process**, not instant.

callouts.p: A character whose qualities contrast with, or warn about, another character's, highlighting that character's traits or choices.
Marley = what Scrooge **will become**. Fezziwig = what Scrooge **could have been**. Fred = the Christmas spirit Scrooge **rejects** and finally **embraces**.

core.h: 3. Marley: the catalyst and the warning (the unredeemed foil)
core.p: Jacob Marley is the **catalyst** that begins Scrooge's transformation and a **foil** who shows what happens to a man who never changes. He was Scrooge's business partner and twin in greed. Dead, he is punished forever, and that is the fate awaiting Scrooge unless he transforms.

bullets: **Ghost of Christmas Past = memory and regret.** Scrooge sees 'a solitary child, neglected by his friends' and weeps 'to see his poor forgotten self as he used to be'. Tears are the first crack in the flint.

Straight after this he regrets frightening the carol singer: 'There was a boy singing a Christmas Carol at my door last night. I should like to have given him something: that's all.' This is his **first act of conscience**.
After Fezziwig's ball he says 'I should like to be able to say a word or two to my clerk just now!' He is already thinking about **Bob**, so the change is beginning.
Belle: 'Another idol has displaced me... a golden one.' The **religious metaphor** (idol) shows money has become his false god. 'Remove me! I cannot bear it!' shows growing **pain at his choices**.

**Ghost of Christmas Present = empathy and social responsibility.** 'Spirit,' said Scrooge, 'with an interest he had never felt before, tell me if Tiny Tim will live.' He feels for someone else for the first time.

The Spirit quotes him: 'decrease the surplus population'. Scrooge 'hung his head to hear his own words quoted by the Spirit, and was overcome with **penitence** and grief'. This is a key moment of **repentance**.
Ignorance and Want: 'Are there no prisons?' is thrown back at him. His own words now condemn him, showing he must take **social**, not just personal, responsibility.
**Ghost of Christmas Yet To Come = fear and resolve.** 'I fear you more than any spectre I have seen.' He sees his unmourned death, the stolen bed-curtains and his gravestone.
'Why show me this, if I am past all hope?' and 'Assure me that I yet may change these shadows you have shown me, by an altered life!' show his desperate wish for **redemption**.
'I am not the man I was.' This **declarative sentence** marks the turning point of his identity.

callouts.p: 'Are these the shadows of the things that Will be, or are they shadows of the things that May be, only?' The future is not fixed. **Free will** makes redemption possible, which links back to Marley forging his chain 'of my own free will'.
callouts.t: Shadows of things that MAY be

callouts.p: Use the phrase **'gradual transformation'** and give evidence from at least two different staves before Stave 5. Examiners reward tracking development across the whole text.

core.h: 4. A gradual transformation: how each Spirit changes Scrooge
core.p: A grade 9 answer argues that Scrooge's change is **gradual and convincing**, built step by step across Staves 2 to 4. Each Spirit works on a different part of him: **memory**, then **empathy**, then **fear**. Together they turn feeling into a firm decision to act.

head: Spirit / Stave
Method of change
Key evidence
What Scrooge gains
rows: 'I wear the chain I forged in life'
'his poor forgotten self'; 'I should like to have given him something'
Self-understanding and the first stirrings of conscience
'tell me if Tiny Tim will live'; 'overcome with penitence and grief'
Compassion and shame at his own words
'I am not the man I was'
A vow to change: 'an altered life'
'as good a man, as the good old city knew'

bullets: 'I will honour Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year. I will live in the Past, the Present, and the Future. The Spirits of all Three shall strive within me.': a **tricolon** and **vow**. Christmas values must last all year, not just one day.

'I am as light as a feather, I am as happy as an angel, I am as merry as a school-boy. I am as giddy as a drunken man.': a **list of similes** shows overflowing joy. 'Light' contrasts with Marley's heavy chain: the weight of sin has been lifted. 'Angel' adds a religious, saved quality.
'I don't know anything. I'm quite a baby... I'd rather be a baby.': **rebirth imagery**. On the day celebrating Christ's birth, Scrooge is spiritually **born again**.
His laugh: 'for a man who had been out of practice for so many years, it was a splendid laugh, a most illustrious laugh.'
He sends the 'prize Turkey' to the Cratchits anonymously: generosity without wanting praise.

To the charity gentleman: 'Not a farthing less. A great many back-payments are included in it.' The phrase **'back-payments'** shows he is **making amends** for past meanness, and 'farthing' echoes his old money-obsession now turned to giving.
At Fred's: 'Wonderful party, wonderful games, wonderful unanimity, wonderful happiness!' **Anaphora** (repetition of 'wonderful') shows his joy at rejoining his family.
To Bob: 'I'll raise your salary, and endeavour to assist your struggling family.' He takes **responsibility as an employer**, like Fezziwig.
'to Tiny Tim, who did NOT die, he was a second father': capitals stress that the future **was** changed.
'He became as good a friend, as good a master, and as good a man, as the good old city knew': **repetition** of 'good' frames his redemption as complete and public.
'Some people laughed to see the alteration in him, but he let them laugh, and little heeded them... His own heart laughed: and that was quite enough for him.'
'it was always said of him, that he knew how to keep Christmas well, if any man alive possessed the knowledge.'

callouts.p: Scrooge proves his redemption through **deeds**, not just words. This reflects the Christian idea that true repentance is shown by changed behaviour, and Dickens's demand that the rich must **actively help** the poor.

Scrooge is still recognisably Scrooge: he plays a trick on Bob for being late ('I am not going to stand this sort of thing any longer') before raising his salary. His sharp wit is now used for **good humour**, so the character feels consistent.

core.h: 5. The 'after': Stave 5 and redemption proved through action
core.p: Stave 5 shows Scrooge's transformation is **real** because he immediately **acts**. Dickens deliberately **mirrors** Stave 1: Scrooge meets the same people and situations again but behaves in the opposite way. This **cyclical structure** lets readers measure exactly how much he has changed.

head: Stave 1 (before)
Stave 5 (after)
What it shows
rows: Bob's tiny fire; grudges Christmas Day off
Sends a boy for the 'prize Turkey' and rewards him
Kindness to the young and poor
'Golden sunlight; Heavenly sky; sweet fresh air'

bullets: **Novella**: short enough to read in one sitting (or aloud to a family at Christmas), so the moral is concentrated and easy to remember.
**Five 'staves'**: a stave is a set of lines in music, so the book is structured like a **carol**, a song of joy and religious celebration. The 'song' ends in harmony when Scrooge is redeemed.
**Cyclical/mirror structure**: Stave 5 revisits Stave 1's characters (Fred, the charity gentlemen, Bob, a boy in the street), so the change is measurable.
**Chronological journey through time**: Past, Present, Future. Understanding where you came from, how others live now, and where your choices lead is Dickens's recipe for change.
**Allegory / morality tale**: Scrooge is an 'Everyman'-type figure for the greedy rich; the Spirits are like moral teachers. Characters such as Ignorance and Want are **allegorical** figures.
**Didactic purpose**: the novella teaches a lesson. Each Stave ends on a turning point, building **tension** and momentum towards redemption.

**Third-person omniscient narrator** with a chatty, intrusive voice ('I am standing in the spirit at your elbow'), which brings the reader close to Scrooge's experience so the reader is 'transformed' too.

**Pathetic fallacy**: fog and freezing cold in Stave 1 versus 'No fog, no mist; clear, bright, jovial, stirring, cold' in Stave 5. Even the cold is now 'piping for the blood to dance to', showing a transformed outlook.
**Light and dark imagery**: the Ghost of Christmas Past's light, which Scrooge tries to extinguish with the cap, versus the bright sunlight of Stave 5. Light = truth and goodness.
**Supernatural form** (ghost story): fear and wonder shock both Scrooge and the reader into reflection.

callouts.p: Intended to teach a moral lesson.
A structure in which the ending returns to or mirrors the beginning, highlighting change or lack of change.
In part (a), linking a single extract detail to its place in the arc (for example 'this moment of penitence in Stave 3 prepares for his vow in Stave 4') shows structural awareness.

core.h: 6. Form and structure: how Dickens shapes the redemption story
core.p: AO2 rewards comments on **form and structure**, not only language. Dickens chose a short, tightly structured form so that the transformation feels like a clear moral journey that readers can follow and learn from.

bullets: **Christianity**: most Victorian readers were Christian. The ideas of **sin, repentance, forgiveness and being 'born again'** were familiar. Scrooge's redemption on Christmas Day mirrors Christian salvation. Dickens stresses practical Christian **charity** rather than strict doctrine.

**The 1834 Poor Law Amendment Act**: poor relief mainly through harsh **workhouses** designed to deter people from seeking help. Scrooge's 'Union workhouses?' shows he supports this system; his redemption means rejecting it and giving personally.

**Malthus**: Thomas Malthus's Essay on the Principle of Population (1798) argued that population growth would outstrip food supply. Scrooge's 'surplus population' echoes this; the Ghost of Christmas Present attacks it, and Scrooge's shame shows he rejects that way of thinking.

**Dickens's own childhood**: when his father was imprisoned for debt in the Marshalsea, the young Dickens worked in a blacking factory. He knew poverty first-hand, which helps explain his anger and his hope that the rich could change.

**1843**: Dickens was angered by reports on child labour (the Children's Employment Commission). He chose to write a story rather than a political pamphlet, believing a story could change hearts more powerfully. Scrooge's redemption is **the model for his readers**.

**Victorian middle-class readers**: the people who could change things were exactly the people who might think like Scrooge. Dickens persuades them gently, through warmth and humour, not attack: the book should 'haunt their houses pleasantly'.
**The Victorian Christmas**: Christmas customs were growing in popularity in the 1840s; Dickens links Christmas with family, generosity and goodwill, making it the perfect moment for transformation.

callouts.p: Always link context to the text: 'Scrooge's echo of Malthus's ideas about surplus population, quoted back to him in Stave 3, shows Dickens attacking a real Victorian attitude and suggesting that the rich, like Scrooge, can be shamed into change.'
A paragraph of history with no link to Scrooge's transformation earns little credit. Context must explain Dickens's **purpose**.

core.h: 7. Context (AO3): why redemption mattered to Dickens and his readers
core.p: Part (b) of the Edexcel question requires you to **refer to the context of the novel**. Context must explain **why** Dickens presents redemption as he does, not just list facts.

bullets: **Is the change too sudden?** Some readers find the transformation unrealistic or sentimental. Counter: Dickens plants seeds from Stave 1 (flint, oyster) and shows small changes in Staves 2 and 3, so it is **gradual and earned**. The overnight timescale suits the genre of the **moral fable**, in which realism is less important than the lesson.

**Fear or love?** Is Scrooge redeemed partly out of **self-interest** (fear of his own death in Stave 4)? Dickens uses both: **empathy** (Tiny Tim, his younger self) and **fear** (his grave). Perhaps Dickens believed his readers also needed both a carrot and a stick.

**Personal or social redemption?** Scrooge saves himself, but his change also saves Tiny Tim and helps the poor. Dickens suggests personal salvation and **social responsibility** cannot be separated, which is Marley's 'Mankind was my business'.
**Free will**: the 'shadows of the things that May be' show that the future is not fixed. Redemption depends on **choice**, so readers are responsible for their own choices.
**The reader's redemption**: the narrator and Preface invite the reader to see themselves in Scrooge. The real transformation Dickens wants is in Victorian society.

**Limits**: Scrooge's redemption depends on individual charity. Some critics argue Dickens offers a **personal, not political**, solution to poverty: one kind employer rather than wider reform. Mentioning this shows sophisticated evaluation.

**Is anyone else transformed?** Most characters (Fred, Bob, the Cratchits) are already good. Their **constancy**, such as Fred's 'I mean to give him the same chance every year... for I pity him', shows that patient kindness helps make redemption possible.

callouts.p: Phrases like 'perhaps Dickens suggests...', 'this could be read as...', 'alternatively...' signal the **exploratory** response that top-band descriptors reward.

core.p: Top-band answers are **critical, exploratory and perceptive**. They offer alternative readings and weigh them up rather than retelling the plot.

bullets: **Part (a)**, 20 marks: 'Explore how Dickens presents...' in the extract. This assesses **AO2** (language, form and structure). Analyse methods closely and use subject terminology accurately.

**Part (b)**, 20 marks: 'Explain the importance of... elsewhere in the novel' with bullet prompts and the instruction to refer to context. This assesses **AO1** (personal response, textual references) and **AO3** (context). Do NOT reuse the extract in part (b).
Learn short, flexible quotations from **every stave** so you can trace the arc in part (b).
Plan your part (b) answer chronologically (Stave 1, 2, 3, 4, 5) or conceptually (causes of change, signs of change, proof of change). Both work if you track development.
Name Dickens's **purpose** in most paragraphs: 'Dickens uses... to show/warn/encourage his readers...'.
Embed quotations and zoom in on single words ('forged', 'penitence', 'baby', 'back-payments').
Spend roughly equal time on (a) and (b) because they carry equal marks.

callouts.p: GCSE English Literature is **not tiered**: everyone sits the same paper. 'Grade 9 depth' comes from perceptive analysis and well-integrated context, not extra content.
(a) = AO2 language, form, structure on the extract. (b) = AO1 and AO3 across the rest of the novel, including context.

core.h: 9. Exam technique for Edexcel 1ET0 Paper 2, Section A
core.p: Edexcel Paper 2 Section A has a two-part question on A Christmas Carol: part (a) on an **extract** and part (b) on the **whole novel**, each worth 20 marks. Redemption can appear as the focus of either part.

model: 'I should like to have given him something: that's all.' (Stave 2, about the carol singer), showing an early stirring of conscience.
'tell me if Tiny Tim will live' / 'overcome with penitence and grief' (Stave 3) / 'I am not the man I was' (Stave 4).
exam.q: (Revision check, not full exam format) Give two quotations that show Scrooge's transformation has begun before Stave 5.
exam.tip: Learn at least one short quotation from every stave so you can show the change is gradual.

model: The chain is a symbol of sin, made of 'cash-boxes, keys, padlocks, ledgers', the tools of greed.
'I wear the chain I forged in life': the verb 'forged' shows Marley created his own punishment.
'of my own free will' stresses personal responsibility, so if sin is chosen, change can also be chosen.
Marley acts as a foil and warning: 'You have yet a chance and hope of escaping my fate', so redemption is still possible for Scrooge while he lives.
exam.q: (Revision check) Explain how Dickens uses Marley's chain to present the possibility of redemption.
exam.tip: Turn a symbol into an argument: what it represents, a key word, and what it means for the theme.

model: Cyclical/mirror structure: Stave 5 revisits Stave 1 situations (Fred, charity collectors, Bob), so the change is measurable.
Example: 'Are there no prisons?' becomes 'Not a farthing less... back-payments'.
The Past, Present, Future sequence builds change step by step: memory, then empathy, then fear.
Each stave ends on a turning point, driving the reader towards redemption.
Five 'staves' create a carol form that ends in harmony and celebration.
Pathetic fallacy shifts from fog and cold in Stave 1 to 'Golden sunlight; Heavenly sky' in Stave 5, mirroring inner change.
exam.q: (Revision check) How does Dickens use the structure of the novella to show Scrooge's transformation? Give three methods.
exam.tip: Structure means the order and arrangement of events, so refer to WHERE things happen in the book.

model: AO2: Analyse the list of similes 'light as a feather... happy as an angel... merry as a school-boy... giddy as a drunken man': lightness contrasts with Marley's heavy chain; 'angel' suggests spiritual salvation.
AO2: Rebirth imagery: 'I'm quite a baby' shows Scrooge spiritually reborn on the day celebrating Christ's birth.
AO2: Exclamations, short sentences and fragmented speech convey overwhelming, childlike joy, in contrast to his clipped 'Bah! Humbug!'.
AO2: The repeated phrase 'They were not torn down' echoes Stave 4's stolen bed-curtains, showing structurally that the future has been changed.
AO2: Comment on the laugh 'out of practice for so many years': humour and warmth replace coldness.
AO2: Pathetic fallacy: 'No fog, no mist... Golden sunlight; Heavenly sky' mirrors Stave 1's fog, reflecting moral change.
AO2: Use accurate terminology (simile, tricolon, exclamative sentences, cyclical structure) and explore the effects on the reader.
Top band: perceptive, detailed analysis of how methods create meaning, with well-chosen, integrated references.
exam.q: (Part a style, extract from Stave 5 beginning 'Yes! and the bedpost was his own...') Explore how Dickens presents Scrooge's transformation in this extract. You must refer to the language, form and structure used in the extract.
exam.tip: Stay inside the extract for part (a). Zoom in on individual words and always explain the effect on the reader.

model: AO1: Stave 1 'before': 'covetous old sinner', 'solitary as an oyster', 'decrease the surplus population', establishing the need for redemption.
AO1: Marley as catalyst and foil: 'I wear the chain I forged in life'; 'Mankind was my business'.
AO1: Gradual change: tears for his 'poor forgotten self'; regret about the carol singer; thoughts of Bob after Fezziwig.
AO1: Stave 3 empathy: 'tell me if Tiny Tim will live'; 'overcome with penitence and grief' when his own words are quoted back.
AO1: Stave 4 fear and resolve: his unmourned death and grave; 'I am not the man I was'; 'shadows of the things that May be' (free will).
AO1: Stave 5 action: 'back-payments', Bob's salary, 'second father' to Tiny Tim, 'as good a man, as the good old city knew'.
AO3: Christian context of repentance and rebirth on Christmas Day.
AO3: The 1834 Poor Law and workhouses, and Malthus's 'surplus population', show Dickens attacking real attitudes among wealthy readers.
AO3: Dickens's purpose in 1843: to change readers' hearts after reports on child poverty; Scrooge models the change he wanted in society.
Top band: critical, exploratory response, for example a debate over whether fear or empathy drives the change, or whether individual charity is enough.
exam.q: (Part b style) In the extract, Scrooge is transformed. Explain the importance of change and redemption elsewhere in the novel. In your answer you must consider: how Scrooge changes; the reasons for this change. You must refer to the context of the novel.
exam.tip: Do not reuse the extract. Track change across several staves and weave context into your argument about Dickens's purpose.

mistakes.r: Scrooge changes gradually: tears and regret in Stave 2, empathy and penitence in Stave 3, fear and a vow in Stave 4, then action in Stave 5. Seeds are planted even in Stave 1.
mistakes.w: Scrooge suddenly changes overnight in Stave 5.

mistakes.r: Dickens presents him as a 'sinner' with hidden potential for good (flint, oyster), making redemption possible and giving the moral its force.
mistakes.w: Scrooge is just an evil character.

mistakes.r: Analyse HOW Dickens presents the change (language, structure, symbols) and WHY (his purpose and context).
mistakes.w: Retelling the plot of each ghost visit.

mistakes.r: Link context to the theme: for example, Scrooge's 'Union workhouses?' reflects the 1834 Poor Law, and his redemption shows Dickens urging the rich to give personally rather than rely on harsh institutions.
mistakes.w: Dickens lived in Victorian times when people were poor. (bolt-on context)

mistakes.r: Redemption is proved by action and making amends: the turkey, the 'back-payments', Bob's raise, becoming 'a second father' to Tiny Tim.
mistakes.w: Scrooge is redeemed just because he feels sorry.

mistakes.r: They are 'shadows of the things that May be': the future can change through free will, which is the whole basis of redemption.
mistakes.w: The Ghost of Christmas Yet To Come shows what WILL happen.

mistakes.r: Part (b) asks about 'elsewhere in the novel'. Use different moments from other staves and include context.
mistakes.w: Using the part (a) extract again in part (b).

mistakes.r: Call them staves and explain the carol link; comment on the novella form and cyclical structure for AO2 credit.
mistakes.w: Calling the chapters 'chapters' and ignoring form.

summary: Redemption and transformation is the central moral of A Christmas Carol: through the visits of Marley and the three Spirits, Dickens takes Scrooge from a cold, isolated, greedy miser to a generous, warm-hearted member of society, showing his Victorian readers that **it is never too late to change** and that true redemption must be proved through **action and social responsibility**.

terms.d: Being saved from sin or wrongdoing, usually through repentance and making amends.
A complete change in a character's nature, attitudes and behaviour.
Sincere regret for wrongdoing, with a wish to change; Scrooge is 'overcome with penitence and grief' in Stave 3.
Putting right the harm you have done, for example Scrooge's 'back-payments' to charity.
Something that triggers change; Marley's visit is the catalyst for Scrooge's transformation.
A character who contrasts with another to highlight their qualities; Marley and Fezziwig are foils to Scrooge.
Designed to teach a moral lesson.
A story in which characters and events represent wider moral or political ideas, for example Ignorance and Want.
A story showing the difference between right and wrong, often with a sinner who learns a lesson.
A prose fiction text longer than a short story but shorter than a novel.
A set of lines for writing music; Dickens's name for his five chapters, linking the book to a carol.
An ending that mirrors the beginning; Stave 5 mirrors Stave 1 to measure Scrooge's change.
Weather or setting reflecting emotions or moral state, such as fog in Stave 1 and golden sunlight in Stave 5.
Hints of later events, such as 'flint' that could spark 'generous fire'.
Linked to Thomas Malthus's view that population growth outstrips resources; echoed in Scrooge's 'surplus population'.
A law making workhouses the main form of poor relief, with deliberately harsh conditions.
Kindness and the wish to do good to others; one of the qualities Marley says was his true 'business'.
A person who dislikes or distrusts other people, as Scrooge is at the start.
A sudden moment of realisation, for example Scrooge's 'I am not the man I was.'
